implementation_notes: The JVM toolkits provide the pattern as a deferred-rendering seam rather than a syntax: ListView's cellFactory property holds a Callback (a function) that the control invokes to create the cell for each item, and the javadoc states that setting a custom cell factory 'has the effect of deferring all cell creation, allowing for total customization of the cell' - the control owns the model state, the caller's callback owns the visuals. Swing's equivalent is ListCellRenderer, whose getListCellRendererComponent receives the value and returns the component to paint. When no cell mechanism fits, hand-write a control exposing an ObjectProperty<Function<State, Node>> and invoke it from the layout pass; prefer the toolkit seam whenever the rendering is item-shaped.
pitfalls: Cells are recycled: constructing nodes inside updateItem - the javadoc explicitly warns against it - creates a node per rebind and destroys scrolling performance; create once in the cell and only update in updateItem.
The cell factory runs lazily and may never run for an empty list, so renderer wiring cannot be verified by construction alone.
A cell factory that ignores its ListView argument loses the ability to adapt to view state such as orientation or selection mode.

variants.name: Swing cell renderer (ListCellRenderer rubber stamp)
variants.implementation_notes: Swing's documented mechanism is a renderer object used as a rubber stamp: the JList hands getListCellRendererComponent the value plus the selection and focus state, and the returned component is painted for the cell - the same shape recurs as TableCellRenderer and TreeCellRenderer. It is the pattern with an object in place of a function: the interface method is the render function, the caller still decides every visual, and the model owns the data. Choose it for Swing screens; for new code prefer the JavaFX cell factory, and hand-write a Function-valued control property only outside both toolkits.
pitfalls: The renderer returns a shared component: storing per-cell state in it or allocating a new component per call misreports preferred sizes; the documented pattern is to reconfigure and return the same stamp.
Selection and focus flags must be honoured in the renderer, which is the only place that knows them; ignoring them strips the list of its affordances.
